newsitem.title: UK: BOE favours modest rate rise now, maybe more later.
newsitem.headline: BOE favours modest rate rise now, maybe more later.

text.p: Bank of England deputy governor Howard Davies said the Bank believed a modest rise in interest rates was needed to ensure the government met its 2.5 percent inflation target.

"We have been talking about a quarter percent in the short term, with perhaps a little more later in the year, the aim being to ensure that the strong growth of domestic demand does not get out of hand," he said in a speech prepared for delivery at a Housing Corporation conference in London.
"You may or may not think this argument persuasive, from where you sit. If you do not, then you must be sitting somewhere close to Kenneth Clarke."
Davies said differences of view between the Bank and Clarke, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, were quite narrow.
"We are talking about differences of a quarter of a percent, here or there, or to put it another way, differences of timing of a month or two in either direction."
Davies said he did not wish to anticipate the Bank's quarterly Inflation Report, which will be published at 1130 GMT on Wednesday, but added:

"Even taking the beneficial effects of the exchange rate rise into account, we are not entirely persuaded that on current interest rates we are on track to meet the government's inflation target of 2.5 percent over the next two years, which is the remit we have been given."
"Lest this observation create unnecessary alarm, I should say that the rise in rates that we think necessary to meet the target is modest."

The present situation was very far from the experience of Britain's last two economic recoveries, when interest rate changes "were often delayed until the point at which a dramatic move of one or two percent was required to get inflation back under control."

"Some of the nervousness felt about potential interest rate rises derives from the fact that, over two or three decades, people were used to the idea in the UK that interest rates rose in jumps of one and two percent and fell in steps of half or a quarter. That is not the territory we now inhabit."
Davies said the current economic recovery had so far been healthy, with steady growth, low inflation and falling unemployment and no deterioration so far in the balance of payments.
"The outlook for growth is, we think, quite positive," he said.

"We think it likely that domestic demand will grow appreciably above its trend growth rate of perhaps two and a half percent in the next year or so, with a pickup in investment and quite robust growth in consumption."
"On the other hand there may be some negative balance of payment impact from the sharp rise in the exchange rate we saw in the last three months of last year."
Davies said rising house prices were a factor which the Bank took into account in assessing the prospects for inflation and they could become a worry.
"A continuing robust rise in house prices would indeed be a matter of concern for us."
But house prices remained low relative to earnings, with average prices now around 3-1/2 times earnings instead of five times in 1990.
"That ratio could move up a little to its long run average and still be consistent with the inflation target," Davies added.

"What we need to watch carefully, though, is any sign that the price acceleration is taking us into the kind of heady territory we explored in the late 1980s, which in retrospect we know to have been an experience which was bound to end in tears, and did."
-- Richard Murphy, London Newsroom 44 171 542 2774
